headline: Penfield's ledge holds bass after dark, blues run the beach in daylight
subhead: Two different games on the same water — nocturnal stripers on the reefs, daytime bluefish mayhem on bunker along the beachfront.
body_markdown:
Here's the call I made Tuesday night and I'd make it again: skip the last two hours of daylight at Penfield and wait for the tide to turn under darkness. Everybody wants to fish the pretty evening light. I want the ebb starting around 9:30, 10 PM, when the reef's been cooking in warm water all day and the bass finally decide it's safe to come up off the rockpile. That's the program right now, and it's the only one that's consistently working for keeper-class fish.

Kings Point is reading 70.9 — that's warm enough to shut daytime bass activity down almost completely west of Norwalk. What that means on the water is simple: the fish haven't left, they've gone nocturnal and they've gone deep. Penfield Reef, the deeper pocket on the north side around 18 to 22 feet, is holding stripers that feed hard on the last two hours of the ebb and the first hour of the flood, dead of night, no moon interference right now with the cycle where it is. I've been anchoring up-current of the reef itself, not on top of it, and drifting live eels back into the structure on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom without snagging rock. Twenty-six to 34 inches has been the range, a couple pushing 20 pounds mixed in on the stronger nights. This isn't a numbers game — two or three fish in three hours is a good night — but they're quality fish and there's basically zero boat traffic to compete with at 11 PM, which by itself makes it worth losing the sleep.

Daytime, the real show is the bluefish, and it's impossible to miss if you're anywhere near the beach from Greenwich Point east through the Norwalk Islands. Bunker schools are pinned tight against the shoreline in the warm surface water and the blues are working them relentlessly — we flagged this exact pattern building last week, said it would keep spreading along the coast as bunker pushed through, and that's exactly what's happened. Now it's a coastwide story and western Sound is right in the middle of it. Poppers and metal — Ava 27s, half-ounce Kastmasters — thrown right into the froth off Greenwich Point and the outer bar at Sheffield Island are getting hit on nearly every cast during an active blitz. These aren't rat blues either, several 4- to 6-pound fish mixed into the schools, enough teeth to justify wire or at minimum a long mono leader if you don't want to keep re-tying. Best window has been mid-morning through early afternoon on the making tide, when the bunker get pushed tight against the beach and the blues pin them against the sand.

Cockenoe Reef is fishing more like a bottom spot than a bass spot right now, and that's fine — porgies out there have been thick on the Cows-adjacent structure and the reef's southern edge, 15 to 25 feet, on green crab and sandworm fished on a simple hi-lo rig during the slower midday tide stages when the bluefish and bass bite goes quiet. If you've got kids or guests aboard who just want bent rods, that's your play — steady action, nothing dramatic, but you're not coming back skunked. Blackfish season's still closed in Connecticut waters through the summer, so those Cockenoe rockpiles are strictly catch-and-release scouting for now, worth noting the spots for when the fall season opens back up.

Fluke have slid into the pattern you'd expect for this time of year — plenty of shorts working the sand between the reefs, but the keeper-class fish have pulled into deeper, cooler water. The channel edge off Sheffield Island in 25 to 30 feet on the tail end of the outgoing has been the more consistent producer, five-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right along the bottom where the current sweeps bait off the flat into the channel. You have to cover ground here — I made four drifts Sunday morning before connecting on a pair over 20 inches, everything else was 16- and 17-inch fish going back.

Boat traffic's been the other variable to manage. Weekend pressure on Penfield and the Norwalk Islands is brutal by 10 AM once the sailing crowd and the day-trip center consoles show up, so if you're targeting the reef bite specifically, either get there at first light before the parking-lot effect starts, or better yet, lean into the after-dark program where you've got the whole structure to yourself.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for this to change through the weekend. The warm surface water isn't going anywhere with this weather pattern holding, so bass stay nocturnal, blues stay the daytime headline as long as bunker keep getting pushed tight to the beach, and fluke stay a deeper-water, stronger-tide proposition. If the wind stays out of the south and the bunker schools hold their position off Greenwich and the islands, I'd expect the blitz pattern to keep spreading east toward Bridgeport over the next several days rather than break up. My money this week is on the midnight ebb at Penfield for quality bass, and first-light poppers off Greenwich Point for the sure thing.
